name: Plato
role: Athenian philosopher (c. 428–348 BC), founder of the Academy
summary: Plato's political dialogues argue that a city should be ruled by those with knowledge of the Good, organised by function and censored to form virtue. The Republic proposes philosopher-rulers with communal property for the guardians; the Laws, later, proposes a mixed constitution under rule of law with fixed property lots and state-enforced religion. Democracy is treated as a deficient regime.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Laws regulates trade tightly: citizens may not engage in retail, buying and selling happens at supervised markets, and credit is restricted; the Republic leaves producers to trade but under rulers' control.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The Laws caps private wealth at four times the basic lot, with any surplus handed to the state and its gods, and the property classes are set by law. This is a wealth limit rather than a tax schedule.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Republic denies the guardian class private property altogether, and the Laws makes house and lot inalienable and subordinate to the city. The state may override property wherever the common good requires.

state-harmful.rationale: Both the Republic and the Laws are detailed blueprints for a strong state meant to make citizens virtuous; Socrates in the Crito owes the laws his life's obedience.

rehabilitation.rationale: The Athenian holds that punishment should aim to make the offender better, setting up a house of reformation, while treating the incurable as beyond reform; punishment is not mere retribution.

traditional-family.rationale: The Republic abolishes family life for the guardians, while the Laws makes marriage compulsory and strongly regulated and honours parents. His views differ by work.

abortion-legal.rationale: The Republic orders that conceptions beyond the age limit be prevented or not brought to light, under state eugenic rules; this is not a legal right of choice.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Laws makes worship of the gods a central civic duty with state-regulated sacrifices, festivals and priests, and treats impiety as a crime.

gradual-change.rationale: The Laws warns that changes even to children's games and music endanger the state and keeps laws stable; this favours caution rather than gradual reform.

free-trade.rationale: In the Laws the city is sited inland, away from the sea, to avoid the commerce that corrupts character; imports, exports and foreign dealings are controlled by magistrates.

open-borders.rationale: The Laws strictly limits who may travel abroad, and screens foreign visitors, while strangers are received only under conditions.

experts-over-public.rationale: Socrates argues that rule should belong to those with knowledge, comparing the statesman to the pilot and doctor, and the Stranger in the Statesman says the true ruler's expertise matters more than consent or law.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The Laws divides the land into 5040 near-equal lots held by citizen households, with a ceiling on wealth, so property is spread among many small holders rather than concentrated.

democracy-best.rationale: Socrates ranks democracy as the second-worst regime, a step before tyranny; the Stranger in the Statesman calls it the weakest of the lawful forms of rule.

direct-votes.rationale: Plato does not trust mass judgement on laws: the Republic gives lawmaking to philosophers and the Laws gives the assembly a limited role under the guardians of the law.

natural-rulers.rationale: Socrates holds that nature produces philosophers fit to rule and others fit to be guardians or producers, and that the city is just only when each person is placed accordingly.

war-builds-character.rationale: The Athenian criticises Spartan and Cretan laws for aiming at war and says that war should serve peace; he does grant that training for danger builds courage.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Laws fuses religion and the state, giving the Nocturnal Council and magistrates the task of enforcing belief in the gods.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Book VIII of the Republic ties regime changes to conflict between rich and poor but makes moral decline of the soul their basis.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Socrates rejects pleonexia, the pursuit of more than one's share, as the mark of injustice, while arguing justice benefits the just person; he does not endorse self-interest as the moral standard.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Socrates says the city is founded for the good of the whole and the Crito subordinates the individual's wishes to the laws; Plato has no doctrine of individual rights to weigh against it.

limit-population.rationale: The Laws sets the citizen body at 5040 and has the legislator keep it fixed by checking or encouraging births, with colonies as outlet.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Socrates makes one person, one task the core of justice and of the city's origin: each should do the single work for which their nature suits them.

harm-principle.rationale: The Republic and the Laws legislate for virtue, censoring poetry, regulating marriage and punishing impiety, which goes far beyond preventing harm to others.

conscription.rationale: The Laws requires all citizens to train for war and to serve, and the Republic sets guardians apart as a military class.

total-state.rationale: The Republic and Laws regulate education, the arts, marriage, religion and property, but the Republic leaves producers' economic life largely alone.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Athenian rejects the common view that a legislator should seek a state as great and rich as possible with the greatest empire by land and sea.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Socrates refutes Thrasymachus's claim that justice is the interest of the stronger, and holds that knowledge of the Good is not a product of power.

universal-morality.rationale: Socrates holds that justice and the Good are objective realities known by reason, and the philosopher is the one who grasps them.

single-common-good.rationale: Socrates says the city aims at the happiness of the whole, not of any class, and that rulers must discover this good through philosophy.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The Republic puts reason in command over appetite and emotion, yet the same works rely on myth, divine inspiration and religious law.

class-collaboration.rationale: Socrates holds that the city is just when each class does its own work in harmony and that rich-versus-poor conflict ruins cities (Book VIII); this speaks of social classes generally, not employers and workers specifically.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Socrates argues that women with the right nature should have the same pursuits as men, while the Laws keeps greater domestic duties for women; the evidence is mixed.

ban-interest.rationale: In the Laws the Athenian lays down that no one may lend money at interest, and that a borrower owes neither capital nor interest if a lender breaks the rule.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Socrates says the best should mate with the best, and the offspring of the inferior or deformed should be put away in secret.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Laws prefers proportionate to numerical equality, saying equal honours for unequals produces inequality, and the Republic ranks natures into classes; neither grants equal rights.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Stranger says the true ruler is defined by knowledge, whether subjects are willing or unwilling; Socrates in the Crito, though, argues that citizens are bound by an implicit agreement with the laws. The evidence is mixed.

separated-powers.rationale: The Laws distributes power among guardians of the law, a council, an assembly, scrutineers and a Nocturnal Council that check one another, though it does not use modern separation language.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Socrates mocks the choice of rulers by lot as a democratic habit and the Stranger denounces it as suited to ignorance, though the Laws uses lot for a final step in some elections.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Socrates would banish poets who tell unworthy tales of gods and heroes and admit only hymns to the gods and praises of good men; the Laws also controls music and poetry.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The Laws sites the city away from the sea and bases citizenship on landholding, treating commerce as a moral hazard; it does not compare country and city life directly.

death-penalty.rationale: The Laws prescribes death for incurable offenders and for grave crimes such as parricide, certain forms of impiety and treason.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Both the Republic and the Laws require uniform education and music and treat innovation in them as dangerous.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Socrates says the founding aim of the city was the happiness of the whole rather than any one class, and the Laws regulates holdings and wealth to serve the city; property is justified by its role in the state.

character-from-environment.rationale: Socrates stresses education in forming character but also holds that natures differ at birth and sorts children into classes.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Statesman says the wise ruler would be better than law, but the Laws later calls the law the master of magistrates and the second-best rule its working model. Latest and fullest view favours law binding rulers.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The Athenian says the best constitution is a mean between monarchy and democracy and that the Laws' mode of election observes this mean; he praises mixing of the principles also in Sparta.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The Laws wants an inland, agriculturally self-supporting city with controlled foreign trade, but it does not call for a colonial bloc closed to all trade, so the fit is partial.

patriotic-education.rationale: The founding myth in the Republic teaches citizens that the land is their mother and nurse, and that they must defend it and each other.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Socrates says the philosopher in a corrupt city should stand aside, but in the ideal city should return to rule from duty.

filial-duty.rationale: The Athenian says parents are owed the first and greatest debt, to be repaid with property, person and soul in return for the care given in infancy.

office-by-exam.rationale: The Republic selects rulers by a long course of education and repeated testing in learning and character, not by popular election; the Laws uses elections, so this is a Republic position.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Socrates calls the luxurious city feverish and says the pursuit of wealth and luxury corrupts the guardians; the Laws limits wealth to make citizens moderate.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: In the Crito Socrates refuses to escape because he owes the laws obedience or persuasion, and holds that he agreed to this by living in Athens.

religion-illusion.rationale: Plato's speakers hold that gods exist and that the soul is immortal (Republic Book X; Laws Book X), not that religion is an illusion.

socialized-care.rationale: The Republic has the guardians' children raised in common by the state, but the Laws returns to the family household.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Athenian in the Laws calls sex between men or between women contrary to nature and proposes a law against it; his earlier dialogues speak differently.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Book X of the Laws sets penalties, up to death, for impiety, including denial of the gods and private shrines, and confines offenders in a house of reformation or a prison.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Athenian presents law as the distribution of reason and traces rule to a divine age under Cronos; in the Republic authority rests on knowledge of the Good rather than on the people.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Socrates says rulers' children who prove base must be demoted and children of lower classes promoted, so office does not pass by descent.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Statesman treats rule by established written law as the second-best constitution, and the Laws gives laws published preambles explaining them to citizens.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Republic (Book VIII) traces the fall of constitutions to the extremes of wealth and poverty, and the Laws bans gold and silver for citizens and caps wealth to prevent faction. Framed as civic stability rather than liberty as such.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Laws treats atheism as the root of impiety, to be refuted by argument and punished.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Socrates says guardians who die bravely in war are to be honoured as demigods, with public memorials and sacrifices.

person-over-state.rationale: The Republic forms individuals to fit the city's good and the Crito places duty to the laws above personal safety; Plato treats persons as parts of the whole.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Socrates in the Republic describes the soul as immortal and the aim of education as turning it towards the Good, and the city exists to care for the soul.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Republic admits women to the guardian and ruler classes on the same terms, and the Laws gives women education, military training and some offices, though not full parity.

simple-living.rationale: Socrates praises the simple first city as the healthy one, and the Laws keeps citizens' wealth limited and bars gold and silver, favouring modest living within a communal order.

equal-conscription.rationale: The Athenian proposes a law that all citizens, male and female alike, attend to military training; the Republic trains women guardians alongside men.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The noble story in the Republic presents the country as a mother whom citizens must defend, a bond taught in education.

notes: Plato wrote dialogues and never speaks in his own voice; positions are those argued and concluded by Socrates (Republic, Crito) and the Athenian Stranger (Laws) and the Eleatic Stranger (Statesman), and scholars note the Republic and Laws differ (Laws gives law and mixed government more weight). Views raised only to be refuted are not attributed to him. Only the four dialogues above were read for answers; other dialogues (for example the Gorgias, Symposium) were not used.
